newsitem.title: JAPAN: Soup ladles a weapon in the fight against the oil.
newsitem.headline: Soup ladles a weapon in the fight against the oil.

text.p: They scooped, sometimes with gloved hands; they slipped on the greasy rocks, sometimes wincing in pain; and they slithered, sometimes into the oil-filled water.
But they never stopped, no matter how cold the wind, no matter how fruitless their efforts might seem.

Using soup ladles, plastic kitchen buckets and garden wheelbarrows, the fisherfolk of this picturesque village fought back on Wednesday against the tide of oil that had lapped on to their shore, threatening a way of life that has supported their community for generations.

While the hum of central-government machinery filled the air around them, Ojima's answer to a disastrous oil spill from a broken Russian tanker was a 200-strong bucket brigade stretching from the water's edge to a scenic coastal road.
The tanker Nakhodka, carrying 19,000 tonnes (133,000 barrels) of heavy fuel oil, broke in two and started leaking oil in the Sea of Japan on January 2.
By Wednesday, 100 km (60 miles) of coastline stretching north from Kyoto Prefecture had been fouled by one of the worst oil spills ever to hit Japan.
At Ojima there were women of all ages, their faces buried under scarves and surgical masks to help keep out the cold -- and the oily smell that permeated despite the strong winds.
It was not the high technology that is the world's image of Japan. It was village Japan at work.

Takeo, a 64-year-old bespectacled woman who is one of the famous Ama divers, passed plastic bucket after plastic bucket to one of her four sisters, who in turn passed it to another down the line. For centuries, such women have been diving for delicacies of the sea, and even in the modern age have eschewed air tanks or snorkels.

The line started in rocky ankle-deep water where other women -- joined by a handful of men -- used kitchen ladles attached to two-metre poles to scoop the goo from the surface of the now-blackened water and transfer it to a bucket.
Even when a ladle broke, the job continued with hands barely protected by kitchen gloves used to scoop out the sludge.
The slimy water was until Tuesday one of the prime spots in a pristine coastline rich in abalone, crab and seaweed, a popular part of the Japanese diet.
"It's all dead now," said Yukiko Michinoshita, newly married wife of a local fisherman.
"We won't be able to dive here for three or four years, maybe never," said fellow bucket-brigade member Takeo, who was too shy to give her last name.
But even as they watched their livelihood potentially drown in a sea of sludge, the women kept up their spirits, breaking into peals of laughter when a bucket when astray, dumping its load.
When a reporter helped adjust the headgear of a woman whose hands were coated in oil, an elderly woman nearby shouted: "Hey, do you want to help me with my mask?"
